data.title: Majcichov – a Great Moravian lowland fortified settlement
data.excerpt: The area of present-day Majcichov was occupied as early as the Palaeolithic, and in the 9th century a Great Moravian lowland fortified settlement with a ground plan of about 220 × 300 m was built here, at an important trading crossroads. Dendrochronology dated its defensive wall to 892 – 893, that is, to the last years of Great Moravia. A geophysical survey of the interior, however, indicated almost no features at all.

children.text: Archaeological find spots suggest that prehistoric people lived in the area of present-day Majcichov as early as the Palaeolithic (35,000 – 8,000 BC). The literature more often mentions the occupation of Majcichov in the Neolithic (from 5,000 to 3,000 BC). In this connection a settlement of the people of the Linear Pottery culture is mentioned. The people of Majcichov most often find traces of their forebears in the Bronze Age (from 1900 – 700 BC), namely of the Lusatian and Velatice cultures. For the Early Iron Age (from 700 – 300 BC) a settlement is known south of Majcichov, already in the cadastral area of the village of Hoste, in the locality known as Malý háj. At the turn of the 5th and 6th centuries AD the Slavs settled here. Among the surviving traces is a settlement with pottery of the Prague type.

children.text: From the 9th century a Great Moravian defensive hillfort is known at Majcichov, running from the local quarter of Palaj towards Vlčkovský háj and covering an area of 3 ha. The archaeological excavation of this hillfort was carried out by the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra in the 1960s and at the beginning of the 21st century. The excavations suggest that the area could even have been as much as 9 ha. The hillfort lay at an important trading crossroads. It is very likely that Majcichov already existed in this period under the name Majtech, as a small hamlet on what is today the local upper street below the church. A watchtower probably stood on the site of the church. A whole network of service hamlets grew up around the Majcichov hillfort. In this period the people of Majcichov adopted Christianity, which after the demise of the hillfort was further consolidated by the Old Hungarians within the Hungarian state, as is again shown by the many Hungarian place names – Farkašín (Vlčkovce), Majthény (Majcichov).

Matej Ruttkay, Eva Fottová and Joachim Henning, in their paper Archeologický výskum včasnostredovekého hradiska v Majcichove (Archaeological excavation of the early medieval hillfort at Majcichov; in Pieta K., Ruttkay A., Ruttkay M.: 2006, Bojná, Hospodárske a politické centrum Nitrianskeho kniežactva, Nitra), state that the founders of the hillfort placed it on a slight rise in the bend of a river branch, which is clearly identifiable on old maps as well as on aerial photographs. This defined the south-western, southern and south-eastern edge of the fortification. That means that the river branch was used as a water-filled ditch (probably after the banks had been steepened). The north-western and north-eastern sides were built without any connection to the original system of river branches. It was therefore possible to build straight ramparts with an artificial ditch. We assume that the stream bed which runs north-west of the hillfort only reached this place later. This is also suggested by the fact that the northern corner of the hillfort was cut by this stream. Today the south-western side of the hillfort also appears almost as a straight line, that is, the hillfort as a whole has a rectangular ground plan (oriented with its longer axis north-west – south-east) and a rounded south-eastern side. The dimensions are approximately 220 × 300 m. Roughly in the middle of the shorter sides, breaks in the rampart can be observed on aerial photographs – probably gateways. The whole area of the hillfort was intensively cultivated in the past, which resulted in a marked lowering of the ramparts. In the north-eastern part the fortification is disturbed by a river meander, observable already on the First Military Survey. It is interesting that on more recent maps the area designated as the hillfort, or as the ramparts, is the land adjoining the hillfort.

The first evaluation excavation took place here in 1961 under the direction of B. Chropovský, and a relatively thick occupation layer and several features were identified – storage pits and clay domed ovens (production features?). Particularly remarkable is the find of part of a thick-walled vessel with a layer of enamel on its base, which the excavator connected with an enamelling workshop. B. Chropovský also cut one section through the rampart, in the south-western, probably unburnt part. At that time the site was also surveyed for the first time, and the plan shows, among other things, that the difference in height between the rampart and its surroundings was at that time almost two metres. One result of these excavations was also the interpretation of the construction of the fortification: “… the rampart was built on both the inner and the outer side of stone walls using a system of box construction filled with small stones and loess, which consolidated the body of the rampart. In front of the rampart was a ditch whose edge (mouth) reached as far as the outer face of the rampart; the rampart collapsed into this ditch. The field evidence, and above all the heavily burnt soil in the better-preserved part of the rampart (probably at the site of the gateway), shows that besides the grillage construction timber was used here on a larger scale, surely to build a palisade”. The excavation also demonstrated that the northern and north-eastern part of the fortification bears traces of marked burning. More recent excavation has likewise shown that the entrance gateways were placed roughly in the middle of the two opposite shorter stretches of wall. A more complex system of anomalies was also identified near the south-eastern break (entrance), which could indicate a more elaborate fortification structure at the gateway.

Geophysical measurements indicated that the construction element of timber boxes may have been used in building the rampart. An interesting result of the geophysical survey of the fortified interior of the hillfort is the fact that essentially no archaeological features are indicated there. Could such a hillfort have existed without sunken features? On contemporary hillforts a relatively large number of sunken features is usual, and after all the excavation of 1961 also recorded several features in the interior. The characterisation of the hillfort as a refuge more or less without settlement features therefore seems improbable. There may be several explanations for this phenomenon. In the first place it is possible that the proximity of the upper level of the groundwater meant that the inhabitants of the hillfort preferred ground-level buildings to sunken ones, and the traces of these are harder to find. It can be assumed, and the archaeological situation suggests it, that at some time after the demise of the hillfort a large quantity of soil material was washed in here, covering the original occupation horizon. Local people who remember it report extensive flooding in the 1950s, and at the same time also several substantial agricultural alterations in the 1950s and 1960s. In that case the archaeological features were not destroyed but, on the contrary, were preserved beneath a layer of mud – not, of course, as they were at the time of the demise, but as they were at the time of the floods. That could then act as a barrier which prevented the geophysical survey from identifying the individual features. This interpretation could also be supported by the fact that only a minimal number of sherds and fragments of metal objects was found on the area of the hillfort during surface survey.
The ditch

On the north-eastern side the original edge of the ditch was clearly recorded. Its maximum recorded depth in relation to the lower – walking – level at the time the rampart was built was 290 cm. This was probably a steepened bank of an original, relatively narrow river branch, which fell away over a stretch 14 m long. After the demise of the hillfort the ditch was gradually filled in. The present artificial and dry channel (a canal) is cut into the fills of the ditch. For that reason its original width cannot be determined.
The stone facing

The foundation grillage reached right up to the break of slope at the upper edge of the ditch – round timbers most often between 15 and 18 cm in width and 480 – 505 cm in length (perhaps sometimes hewn), laid side by side at right angles to the line of the rampart. Where it met the edge of the ditch the end of the grillage was underlaid by a transverse beam. Above the grillage, in the north-eastern part, only the collapse of the rampart survived, together with an approximately 20 cm thick layer of clayey soil on which rested the remains of the stone facing (85 – 110 cm wide), built of dry-laid stones. Two possibilities come into consideration in interpreting this situation. Variant A – the entire original width of the facing was recorded (85 – 110 cm); in that case there would have had to be a free space 95 – 140 cm wide on the outer side of the hillfort between the facing and the start of the ditch, “paved” with part of the foundation grillage. A kind of outer berm would thus have been created. This element could have had a certain stabilising effect, that is, unlike a wall standing directly on the edge of the ditch, there would have been less danger of it slipping into the ditch. Variant B – it cannot be ruled out that the original facing was wider – possibly as wide as the entire outer width of the timber grillage (between 190 and 230 cm in all). In that case the facing narrowed gradually towards the top. Its front part may have collapsed into the ditch (at least two phases of collapse were recorded). The upper part of the wall, however, clearly collapsed first into the interior of the hillfort.
The box

On the north-eastern side the construction of the box rested on the foundation timber grillage, and on the south-western side on the subsoil. The lower part of the horizontal boarding survived relatively well, especially on the south-western side, where it was sunk about 20 cm into the subsoil. From the inside the structure was strengthened by massive vertical posts. The boarding probably consisted of hewn timber beams about 15 – 22 cm in diameter. In trench II the remains of a transverse tie between the inner and outer boarding were also uncovered. This tie lay exactly opposite the vertical load-bearing post and was likewise recorded only once in the stretch examined, which suggests that the span between these ties was at least 460 cm. The inner fill of the box, 380 – 410 cm wide, consisted of clayey soil. In several places “loaves” of yellow clay were uncovered, strikingly similar to unfired brick. Traces of an inner grillage were also recorded, but this was laid only inside the box and was tied neither to the inner nor to the outer boarding. Remains of various timbers thrown in crosswise also came to light. All the woods analysed pointed to the massive use of oak.
The finds

Despite the archaic character of the pottery found, which suggests a dating perhaps as early as the 8th century, the finds can only provisionally be placed broadly in the 8th to 10th centuries. The find of glass could indicate that the hints of glass production identified by B. Chropovský need not be merely a coincidence, but genuine evidence of craft production on the hillfort. An earlier dating of the hillfort would also be supported by the spur which A. Ruttkay lists in his synthetic study. So far, any more precise chronological placing of the hillfort within this interval is purely speculative. The question of the existence of a settlement, or settlements, in the microregion of the hillfort is an interesting one. Surface survey confirmed the presence of early medieval sherds west of the hillfort and immediately beyond the ditch north of the hillfort. The presence of settlement features was also confirmed here by geophysical and surface archaeological survey. Both settlements are separated from the hillfort by a former river branch or by the ditch. One is north and the other south-west of the hillfort. Unfortunately, it is not yet possible to decide definitively whether they are chronologically connected with the hillfort. A third settlement was discovered by surface collection about 300 m north-east of the hillfort, on a slight rise enclosed on three sides by a river or stream branch. Particularly interesting is the settlement south-west of the hillfort – between the hillfort and the river terrace. The results of geomagnetic measurements suggest that it may have been enclosed by a rampart (if this rampart was not an outwork of the hillfort) and may have formed a kind of bailey.
Dating

During the excavation timber samples were taken from the construction of the rampart and were subsequently subjected to dendrochronological analysis in Germany. Its results are published in the 2011 volume Frühmittelalterliche Burgwälle an der mittleren Donau im ostmitteleuropäischen Kontext. The wall is dated there to 892 – 893, and so the building of the hillfort, or its reconstruction, may be connected with the last years of the existence of Great Moravia.
As the illustration shows, archaeologists reckon with two variants of the appearance, or rather the construction, of the wall, designated Variant A and B.

• Variant A – the entire original width of the facing was recorded (85 – 110 cm); in that case there would have had to be a free space 95 – 140 cm wide on the outer side of the hillfort between the facing and the start of the ditch, “paved” with part of the foundation grillage. A kind of outer berm would thus have been created. This element could have had a certain stabilising effect, that is, unlike a wall standing directly on the edge of the ditch, there would have been less danger of it slipping into the ditch.

children.text: • Variant B – it cannot be ruled out that the original facing was wider – possibly as wide as the entire outer width of the timber grillage (between 190 and 230 cm in all). In that case the facing narrowed gradually towards the top. Its front part may have collapsed into the ditch (at least two phases of collapse were recorded). The upper part of the wall, however, clearly collapsed first into the interior of the hillfort.

The hillfort at Majcichov belongs to the group of lowland fortified settlements. The occurrence of this type in the Early Middle Ages and at the beginning of the High Middle Ages in western Slovakia is not rare. Sites where they occur include, for example, Mužla-Čenkov, Brodské-Veleš, Bíňa and Piešťany-Kocúrice. In most cases the state of knowledge about them is unsatisfactory, and some of them cannot at present be reliably located (Piešťany-Kocúrice). Despite their apparent similarity, their differences must be taken into account, and in many respects these are quite marked – size/area, the massiveness of the fortification, the “infrastructure” and so on. It is also very likely that several lowland fortified settlements were completely destroyed in the past by active agricultural activity and by economic and technical alterations of the land. It must be assumed that, as in southern Moravia, lowland fortified settlements also held an important position in western Slovakia – whether as organisational and administrative centres, or as trading and production centres, or possibly as refuges.
